transcript: I've never been to Kansas, but it's not the first place I’d think you would find eight Asian people simultaneously in the same diner by happenstance. But this is precisely the case in Bus Stop, a co-production between Classic Stage Company, the National Asian American Theatre Company, and Transport Group of the 1955 William Inge play. Taking place over the course of one snowy night where a handful of bus passengers are taking shelter in a small diner, this is a play that highlights an eclectic group of characters passing the time, getting to know each other, and working through whatever is currently going on in their lives. Some share their aspirations and desires, others share their pasts and their regrets. It's a romantically quaint and funny snapshot of Middle America. With an all-Asian-American cast, this production is really intriguing and subversive in that these characters are pretty antithetical to some common Asian stereotypes such as meekness or politeness. But these deeply American characters, who some might consider boisterous or unsophisticated, are no less desperate for meaning and connection than anyone else. That universal theme is really well-rendered in this production, illustrating how it traverses cultural, temporal, and geographic barriers. And all the performances in this production are great. Every character is well-defined, and that allowed me to invest in them more than I thought I would for how far removed they are from me on paper. Overall, I was glad to spend the evening getting to know them, and I honestly would have liked to know them even more. With that, another program for my collection.
